summary: Describes how to use the Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen identity-based encryption algorithms in the Cryptographic Message Syntax to protect content-encryption keys. It defines object identifiers and how to encode a recipient's identity. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5409 shows how to encrypt a message key with identity-based encryption and carry the result in a standard CMS message. It defines the extra fields needed, the object identifiers, and what the sender and the receiver each have to do.

subtitle: Carrying identity-based encryption inside the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

tldr.problem: With ordinary public-key encryption, the sender has to know the recipient's public key, which means a directory or a key lookup before the message can be encrypted.
tldr.mechanism: Identity-based encryption derives the public key from the recipient's identity itself. The document defines how to place that identity, and the encrypted content-encryption key, into the OtherRecipientInfo field of a CMS EnvelopedData structure.
tldr.outcome: The document defines the object identifiers, the ASN.1 syntax and the steps for the sender and the receiver. The system depends entirely on TLS to protect the exchange with the key servers.

today: RFC 5409 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It defines how to carry identity-based encryption inside CMS. The algorithms themselves are in RFC 5091 and the architecture in RFC 5408.

sections.title: Introduction and the IBE Components
sections.content:
This document defines the way to use the Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen identity-based encryption public-key algorithms in the Cryptographic Message Syntax. Identity-based encryption is a public-key technology for encrypting content-encryption keys (CEKs) that can be implemented within the CMS framework: the recipient's identity is incorporated into the EnvelopedData content type using the OtherRecipientInfo CHOICE in the RecipientInfo field. The document does not describe the implementation of the BF and BB1 algorithms themselves, which are described in RFC 5091.

IBE algorithms are a type of public-key cryptographic algorithm in which the public key is calculated directly from a user's identity instead of being generated randomly. This requires a different set of steps for encryption and decryption than other public-key algorithms, and those steps are defined in sections 4 and 5. The document also defines the object identifiers and the syntax of the object used to define the identity of a message recipient, and both the CMS values and the identity objects are defined using ASN.1.

Beyond the client components, a complete IBE messaging system needs two more. The Private-Key Generator (PKG) holds the cryptographic material, known as a master secret, for generating an individual's IBE private key. It accepts a private key request and, after successfully authenticating the requester in some way, returns their private key. The Public Parameter Server (PPS) provides publicly sharable cryptographic material, known as IBE public parameters, and the policy information for the PKG, at a well-known location for distribution.

All communications between users of an IBE system and the PPS or PKG MUST be protected using TLS, as described in RFC 5408. That provides confidentiality and integrity for the information delivered to users, and authenticates the PPS and the PKG.
sections.plainLanguage: With ordinary public-key encryption, the sender needs the recipient's public key, which lives in a directory or a certificate. With identity-based encryption, the public key is computed from the recipient's identity, so the sender can encrypt straight away. Two extra servers are needed: one that publishes the system parameters, and one that holds the master secret and hands out private keys to users it has authenticated.

sections.title: Encoding the Recipient in CMS
sections.content:
To use IBE, the ori field in RecipientInfo MUST be used. oriType is set to ibeORIType and oriValue is set to ibeORIValue. The oriType object identifier indicates that the following oriValue holds the information needed to decrypt the message using IBE, and it is set to a value under the joint-iso-itu-t country us organization identicrypt arc, with the components ibcs, cms, ori-oid and version.

The oriValue is an IBERecipientInfo type. Its cmsVersion MUST be set to 3. The keyFetchMethod is the object identifier that defines the method of retrieving the private key the recipient MUST use, and it SHOULD be set to uriPPSOID, which points at the location of the public parameter server. The recipientIdentity is the data the sender used to calculate the IBE public key used to encrypt the content-encryption key, and it is used to calculate IBE public and private keys as described in RFC 5091. It MUST be a DER-encoded IBEIdentityInfo type, which is a sequence of a district string, a serial integer, an identityType object identifier and an identityData octet string.

The identityType defines the format used to encode the information that defines the identity of the recipient, and it MUST be set to cmsIdentityOID to indicate that identityData contains an EmailIdentityData type. The identityData MUST be an EmailIdentityData type, which is a sequence of an rfc822Name string and a time. The rfc822Name is the email address of the recipient in the format defined for the rfc822Name subjectAltName variant, and the rules for encoding addresses that include internationalized domain names are the ones specified for that profile.

The time field is the UTC time after which the sender wants to let the recipient decrypt the message, so it may be called the not-before time. It is usually set to the time when the message is encrypted but MAY be set to a future time. It MUST be expressed in Greenwich Mean Time, MUST include seconds, so times are always YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ even where the number of seconds is zero, and MUST be expressed to the nearest second.

The sender may round this time to a time interval to create a key lifetime. A key lifetime reduces the number of IBE private keys a recipient needs to retrieve, while still forcing the user to re-authenticate periodically, because the recipient would only have to retrieve a new IBE key once during the interval. The algorithm is: find the GeneralizedTime for the not-before value, convert it to the number of seconds since January 1, 1970 to give the total-time, calculate reduced-time as the floor of the total-time divided by the time-interval, multiplied by the time-interval, and convert reduced-time back to a GeneralizedTime. The worked example starts from 20020401000000Z, giving a total-time of 1017612000, and with a one-week interval of 604800 seconds the reduced-time is 1017273600, which is 20020328000000Z.

When issuing IBE private keys, a PKG SHOULD NOT issue them too far into the future, to stop an adversary who obtains a user's authentication credentials from requesting private keys far ahead and negating the periodic re-authentication that a key lifetime provides. If a one-week period is chosen, private keys should not be issued more than one week in advance, since once an adversary gains access to the PKG with the stolen credentials they can request all future keys.

The serverInfo is an optional sequence of object identifier and value pairs, which can convey any other information that might be used by the PKG, such as the user interface the recipient will experience, including localization or commercial branding. A client MUST ignore any part of serverInfo that it cannot process. The encryptedKey is the result of encrypting the CEK with an IBE algorithm using recipientIdentity as the IBE public key.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipient's details go into a new field of the CMS recipient information. The field carries the identity used to derive the key, an email address and a time before which the message should not be opened, and the encrypted message key itself. Rounding the time down to a fixed interval means a user only has to fetch a new private key once per interval, while still having to prove who they are each time.

sections.title: Key Encryption Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content: The BF and BB1 algorithms as defined in RFC 5091 have object identifiers, which are also defined in the ASN.1 module in that RFC. The bf identifier sits under the joint-iso-itu-t country us organization identicrypt arc, with the components ibcs, ibcs1, ibe-algorithms and bf. This is the object identifier that MUST be inserted in the keyEncryptionAlgorithm field in the CMS when the BF algorithm is used to encrypt the CEK. The bb1 identifier sits under the same arc with the components ibcs, ibcs1, ibe-algorithms and bb1, and MUST be inserted in the keyEncryptionAlgorithm field when BB1 is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the two algorithms has its own object identifier, and that identifier is what goes into the CMS field that says how the message key was encrypted. It tells the receiver which algorithm to run and which public parameters to fetch.

sections.title: Processing by the Sender and the Receiver
sections.content:
The sender performs the following steps. It selects a set of IBE public parameters to use, in accordance with its local security policy, and determines the URI where those parameters can be obtained, which information MUST be encoded in the IBEIdentityInfo. It sets the fields of an OtherRecipientInfo object to their appropriate values. It calculates an IBE public key using this IBEIdentityInfo as the identity information, and that public key is used to encrypt the content-encryption key. It sets encryptedKey to the IBE-encrypted CEK, and within the CMS the keyEncryptionAlgorithm MUST then be set to the appropriate object identifier for the algorithm used.

On receiving a message with an IBE-encrypted CEK, the recipient determines that the CEK is IBE-encrypted by noting that the oriType of the OtherRecipientInfo type is set to ibeORIType, and determines that the recipientIdentity was used as the identity in the IBE encryption. It determines the location of the IBE public parameters and the IBE Private Key Generator, obtains the public parameters from that location, obtains the IBE private key needed to decrypt the encrypted CEK, and decrypts the CEK using that private key and the algorithms described in RFC 5091.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender looks up the system parameters, computes the recipient's public key from the identity in the message, and uses it to encrypt the message key. The receiver recognises the message as IBE by the type marker, fetches the same parameters and its own private key, and decrypts the message key with it.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
The document ends with an ASN.1 module that summarises the definitions it makes. The module itself is identified under the joint-iso-itu-t country us organization identicrypt arc with the components ibcs, cms, module and version, and it imports IBEIdentityInfo and uriPPSOID from the IBEARCH module.

The module defines IBEOtherRecipientInfo as a sequence of an oriType object identifier and an oriValue of type IBERecipientInfo. It defines IBERecipientInfo as a sequence of cmsVersion, an integer whose only value is v3(3); keyFetchMethod, an object identifier; recipientIdentity, of type IBEIdentityInfo; an optional serverInfo, a sequence of OIDValuePairs of size 1 to MAX; and encryptedKey, of type EncryptedKey. OIDValuePairs is a sequence of a fieldID object identifier and a fieldData octet string, and EncryptedKey is an octet string. It also defines EmailIdentityData as a sequence of an rfc822Name IA5String and a time GeneralizedTime, and the cmsIdentityOID object identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The last section gives the formal definition of every structure the document introduces, so that an implementer can generate matching code from it. The important shapes are the recipient information, which holds the version, the key fetch method, the identity, optional server information and the encrypted key, and the identity data, which holds the email address and the not-before time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document is based on the CMS, IBCS and IBE specifications, and the relevant security considerations of those documents apply. Attacks on the cryptographic algorithms used to implement IBE are outside its scope; those are detailed in RFC 5091, which defines parameters giving 80-bit, 112-bit, 128-bit and 256-bit encryption strength, and the document assumes that capable administrators will select parameters that resist cryptanalytic attack.

Attacks that give an adversary access to or the ability to change the information on a PPS or PKG, especially the master secret, defeat the security of an IBE system, because a compromised master secret lets the adversary recreate any user's private key and decrypt all messages protected with the corresponding public key. It is therefore highly RECOMMENDED that best practices for physical and operational security be followed and that these servers be hardened in accordance with best current practices, and that an IBE system be operated where illicit access is infeasible. Attacks requiring administrative access or IBE-user-equivalent access to client or server machines are also out of scope, and the document assumes that administrators are trustworthy and will not abuse their authority, which is of particular importance with IBE because an administrator of a PKG could configure it to grant himself any private key it is capable of calculating. A system implementing IBE SHOULD implement n-out-of-m control for critical administrative functions and SHOULD maintain auditable logs of all security-critical events.

Attacks within the scope of the document are those that let an adversary passively monitor information transmitted between users and the PPS and PKG, masquerade as a PPS or PKG, perform a denial-of-service attack on a PPS or PKG, or easily guess an IBE user's authentication credential. All communications between users and the PPS or PKG are protected using TLS, and the IBE system provides no additional security for those communications, so it is completely dependent on TLS for server authentication and for the confidentiality and integrity of the exchange. The protocols do not explicitly defend against an attacker masquerading as a legitimate PPS or PKG and rely on the server authentication mechanism of TLS, and client software can add protection by giving users a way to see that a connection to those servers is legitimate.
sections.plainLanguage: The security of the whole system rests on two things. The master secret at the key server must never be stolen, because whoever holds it can recreate anyone's private key. And every exchange with the parameter and key servers must go over TLS, because this protocol adds no protection of its own to that path.

viz.caption: THE COMPONENTS OF AN IDENTITY-BASED ENCRYPTION SYSTEM

children.label: Authenticates the user and returns their private key
Holds the policy information for the PKG
Computes the public key from the recipient identity
Encrypts the content-encryption key with it
Obtains its private key from the PKG

viz.caption: THE IBERECEIPTIENTINFO STRUCTURE DEFINED IN RFC 5409

data.title: IBERecipientInfo
data.code:
IBERecipientInfo ::= SEQUENCE {
  cmsVersion         INTEGER { v3(3) },
  keyFetchMethod     OBJECT IDENTIFIER,
  recipientIdentity  IBEIdentityInfo,
  serverInfo         SEQUENCE SIZE (1..MAX) OF
    OIDValuePairs OPTIONAL,
  encryptedKey       EncryptedKey
}

viz.caption: WHAT THE IDENTITY AND RECIPIENT FIELDS CARRY

items.title: rfc822Name
items.text: The recipient's email address, in the form defined for the rfc822Name subjectAltName.

items.title: time
items.text: The not-before time, in UTC and always written as YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ.

items.title: identityType
items.text: Set to cmsIdentityOID, meaning that the identity data holds an EmailIdentityData value.

items.title: serverInfo
items.text: Optional extra information for the key generator, such as the interface the recipient will see. A client must ignore what it cannot process.

items.title: encryptedKey
items.text: The content-encryption key encrypted with the IBE algorithm, using the recipient identity as the public key.
